doc.title: Jane Jarvis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Jazz festival and scholarship honoring her 80th birthday
summary: Jarvis describes the November festival in her honor, organized by Jazz Music Education, Inc., and the Jane Jarvis Jazz Piano Scholarship aimed at building jazz audiences among young people.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: We are filming today for part of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive project. And it’s a special day for us because today we have with us Jane Jarvis, and I barely know where to start with you. We could do I think about five or six separate interviews with the things you’ve done in your career. But I hope to get to some of those, anyway. Could I start out right now and tell us about this event you have coming up in November. It sounds so exciting.

Oh, I’m really delighted you asked about that because I’ve been preening myself ever since I was told that this was going to take place. A group of people, a small group of people, they began about three years ago asking me if they couldn’t do this. And by this I mean have a jazz festival in my honor. I don’t think it was altogether because of me, I think it was largely because they felt that women had been sort of passed over in jazz. And I just was lucky enough to be the person they chose to start this wonderful thing. So this is a jazz, a bona fide jazz festival, a three day affair, and it is being organized by Jazz Music Education, Inc., a group of interested people who worry about the eventuality of jazz and feel that the place to start is not only in colleges but as early as grade school and even kindergarten. And they feel that we should try to interest more people in the education part of jazz, as opposed to, in addition to performing. Because most of the degrees now that are given in jazz, I think I’m speaking with some knowledge of it, are people who are getting a degree actually in their instrument or in arranging in order to make a livelihood. But what we have been ignoring is the audience. Who is going to be the audience? And it seemed to me and it has to them, the Jazz Music Education folks, that if it could be introduced at a very young age, and you don’t have to make an announcement and say “We are now going to hire a public school teacher who is going to insidiously teach jazz to children.” But it can be done without so saying, just by exposure.
Yeah. So it’s not, so it’s something that’s kind of weaved into the fabric.

Yeah. It doesn’t have to be a rigid attempt. That is what they’re hopeful for. So they are establishing what they call a Jazz Music Education Scholarship. They’re calling it the Jane Jarvis Jazz Piano Scholarship because it seems that most people understand that the real foundation instrument, tonality instrument, is jazz, or rather is piano. And they felt that in the beginning the more people who were interested in jazz piano that they could also be interested in the education of jazz. That it would be one step forward in that area that I spoke of. Now just, this is really almost a new concept in a way. And so just how far they’re going to get with this, it may be that they’ll have to alter the — the goal will always be the same but just how to attain it. At any rate, they have formed this not-for- profit organization and they have determined that they’re going to operate it for a period of five years at the least. And by that time they hope to have this scholarship well established and be making an impact.
Well it looks like an exciting event. You have some great guests coming in, and I hope I can get there.

Oh, I hope you can too, Monk, it’s really going to be — the men that are playing are all men that I’ve worked with. They represent my life in music, actually. And did I mention that it will be my 80th birthday on that Saturday?
Probably someone will play “Happy Birthday” that weekend I think, in an interesting arrangement I bet.
